{{DISPLAYTITLE:Terms, types and judgments}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Checking instead of convincing|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Propositions as types}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Lean's logic is a dependent type theory. Everything in it, a number, a function, a type, a
proposition, a proof, is a '''term''', and the theory consists of rules that say which terms
have which types. This page sets out the basic statement the rules are about, the typing
judgment; the contexts it is made in; the small term language that Lean's kernel actually
receives; the way that language writes bound variables; and the difference between checking
a type and inferring one. The later Foundations pages add one feature at a time to what is
set out here.

== The typing judgment ==

The basic statement of the theory is the '''typing judgment'''

:<math>\Gamma \vdash e : A</math>

read "in the context <math>\Gamma</math>, the term <math>e</math> has type <math>A</math>".
A '''context''' is a list of variables with their types,
<math>x_1 : A_1, \ldots, x_n : A_n</math>, in which each type may mention the variables
before it. A term is '''well-typed''' when some judgment of this form can be derived for it,
and only well-typed terms have a meaning.<ref name="refman-ts">''The Lean Language
Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, chapter 4, "The Type System".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/</ref>

A judgment is not a proposition inside the theory. It is a statement about the theory, made
by its rules. A '''derivation''' is a finite tree of rule applications whose root is the
judgment in question. Lean does not store derivations. Its terms carry enough information,
binder types included, for a derivation to be reconstructed from the term alone, so the term
itself is the evidence; this is what makes a proof term something an independent program can
check.<ref name="refman-ts" />

Two further judgments travel with the first. <math>\Gamma \vdash e \equiv e'</math> says that
two terms are '''definitionally equal''': equal by computation, without proof. And
<math>\Gamma\ \mathrm{ok}</math> says that a context is well formed. A precise presentation
of all three for Lean, with every rule written out, is Carneiro's thesis ''The Type Theory of
Lean''.<ref name="carneiro2019">Mario Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', MSc thesis,
Carnegie Mellon University, 2019. https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref>
The thesis describes Lean 3. The Lean 4 kernel extends that theory with natural-number
literals, nested inductive types, primitive projections and eta for structures. Carneiro
notes that two of these, nested inductive types and eta for structures, change the theory
enough that the 2019 soundness proof does not apply to Lean 4 directly.<ref name="lean4lean">Mario Carneiro, "Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean,
in Lean", in ''31st International Conference on Types for Proofs and Programs (TYPES 2025)'',
LIPIcs vol. 384, pp. 2:1–2:23, 2026. https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2025.2 (read in
the version arXiv:2403.14064v2)</ref>

== Contexts ==

A context is built one variable at a time, and each new variable must be given a type:

:<math>\frac{}{\cdot\ \mathrm{ok}} \qquad \frac{\Gamma\ \mathrm{ok} \qquad \Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u}{\Gamma, x : A\ \mathrm{ok}}</math>

The empty context is well formed, and a well-formed context may be extended by <math>x : A</math> when
<math>A</math> is itself a well-typed term whose type is a universe,
<math>\mathrm{Sort}\,u</math>. Universes are the subject of
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Universes and Prop|Universes and Prop]]; here it is enough
that "<math>A</math> has type <math>\mathrm{Sort}\,u</math> for some <math>u</math>" is what
"<math>A</math> is a type" means. A variable then has the type the context gives it:

:<math>\frac{(x : A) \in \Gamma}{\Gamma \vdash x : A}</math>

This is the form of the variable rule that Carneiro shows can take the place of a separate
weakening rule.<ref name="carneiro2019" />

== The core term language ==

Lean's surface syntax, with its notation, implicit arguments, pattern matching and tactics,
is not what the Lean kernel checks. The elaborator translates it into a much smaller language,
and that smaller language is the data type <code>Lean.Expr</code>. Lean can print its own
definition:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
import Lean
#print Lean.Expr
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints twelve constructors:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Lean.Expr : Type
number of parameters: 0
constructors:
Lean.Expr.bvar : Nat → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.fvar : Lean.FVarId → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.mvar : Lean.MVarId → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.sort : Lean.Level → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.const : Lean.Name → List Lean.Level → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.app : Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.lam : Lean.Name → Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr → Lean.BinderInfo → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.forallE : Lean.Name → Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr → Lean.BinderInfo → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.letE : Lean.Name → Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr → Bool → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.lit : Lean.Literal → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.mdata : Lean.MData → Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr
Lean.Expr.proj : Lean.Name → Nat → Lean.Expr → Lean.Expr
</pre>

Read as a grammar, they are:

* '''<code>bvar</code>''': a bound variable, written as a number (next section).
* '''<code>fvar</code>''': a free variable, named by a unique identifier. The Lean kernel creates these itself when it works under a binder; they do not occur in terms submitted to it.<ref name="lean4lean" />
* '''<code>mvar</code>''': a metavariable, a hole the elaborator has yet to fill. Terms sent to the Lean kernel contain none.<ref name="lean4lean" /> Metavariables belong to [[Lean theorem prover/System/Metavariables and unification|metavariables and unification]].
* '''<code>sort</code>''': a universe <math>\mathrm{Sort}\,u</math>, for a universe level <math>u</math>.
* '''<code>const</code>''': a constant, that is, a definition, theorem, axiom, inductive type, constructor or recursor in Lean's environment, its table of definitions and theorems, together with the universe levels at which it is used.
* '''<code>app</code>''': application of a function to one argument. A function of several arguments is applied one argument at a time.
* '''<code>lam</code>''': a function abstraction, <math>\lambda x : A.\, e</math>, with the binder's name, its type and its body.
* '''<code>forallE</code>''': a dependent function type, <math>(x : A) \to B</math>. Implication, universal quantification and ordinary function types are all this one constructor ([[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Dependent function types|Dependent function types]]).
* '''<code>letE</code>''': a local definition, <math>\mathrm{let}\ x : A := v;\ e</math>.
* '''<code>lit</code>''': a natural-number literal or a string literal, stored directly rather than as a chain of constructors.
* '''<code>mdata</code>''': annotations for the elaborator and printer, which the Lean kernel ignores.
* '''<code>proj</code>''': the <math>i</math>-th field of a value of a structure type.

The names stored in <code>lam</code>, <code>forallE</code> and <code>letE</code>, and the
<code>BinderInfo</code> that marks an argument implicit or explicit, matter only to the
elaborator and the printer; they play no part in type checking.<ref name="lean4lean" />

== Bound variables and de Bruijn indices ==

The Lean kernel does not identify a bound variable by its name. It uses a '''de Bruijn index''':
the number of binders between the variable's occurrence and the binder that introduces
it, so that the nearest binder has index 0; de Bruijn's own numbering also counted the
introducing binder, and so started at 1.<ref name="debruijn1972">N. G. de Bruijn, "Lambda calculus notation with nameless
dummies, a tool for automatic formula manipulation, with application to the Church-Rosser
theorem", ''Indagationes Mathematicae (Proceedings)'' 75(5), 1972, pp. 381–392.
https://doi.org/10.1016/1385-7258(72)90034-0</ref> Lean can show the term it stores for a
small definition:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
open Lean Meta

def apply1 (x : Nat) (f : Nat → Nat) : Nat := f x

#eval show MetaM Unit from do
  let some e := (← getEnv).find? ``apply1 |>.bind (·.value?) | throwError "no value"
  IO.println (repr e)
</pre>

The output is

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Lean.Expr.lam
  `x
  (Lean.Expr.const `Nat [])
  (Lean.Expr.lam
    `f
    (Lean.Expr.forallE
      (Lean.Name.mkNum `a._@._internal._hyg 0)
      (Lean.Expr.const `Nat [])
      (Lean.Expr.const `Nat [])
      (Lean.BinderInfo.default))
    (Lean.Expr.app (Lean.Expr.bvar 0) (Lean.Expr.bvar 1))
    (Lean.BinderInfo.default))
  (Lean.BinderInfo.default)
</pre>

The body <code>f x</code> has become <code>app (bvar 0) (bvar 1)</code>: index 0 is the
nearest enclosing binder, <code>f</code>, and index 1 the next one out, <code>x</code>. The
names <code>x</code> and <code>f</code> survive only as labels on the binders. The type
<code>Nat → Nat</code> appears as a <code>forallE</code> whose bound variable has an internal
name and is never used: an ordinary function type is a dependent function type that does not
depend.

Indices make two terms that differ only in the names of bound variables the same data apart
from those labels, which comparison ignores, so renaming never has to be checked, and substitution cannot capture a variable by
accident. When the Lean kernel needs to work under a binder it replaces the bound variable by a
fresh free variable carrying the binder's type, does its work, and abstracts the free
variable back into an index afterwards. This mixture of indices for bound variables and
names for free ones is called the '''locally nameless''' representation.<ref name="lean4lean" /><ref name="bailey">Christopher
A. Bailey, with contributions from the Lean community, ''Type Checking in Lean 4'' (online
book), chapters "Type Inference" and "Declarations".
https://ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4/</ref>

== The rules ==

With contexts and terms in place, the typing rules for the base language are short. Each is
written with its premises above the line and its conclusion below. They follow the variant
of Carneiro's presentation that has no weakening rule, with <math>\mathrm{Sort}\,u</math> for
his <math>\mathrm{U}_u</math>. In that variant the variable and universe rules apply in any
context, and the constant rule is written here in the same way; that the context is well
formed is checked separately, by the two rules above, and a typing judgment counts only when
its context is well formed.<ref name="carneiro2019" /> Without
weakening, a well-typed body no longer shows that the type of its binder is a type, so the
abstraction rule here also requires <math>A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u</math>, as Lean's kernel
does.<ref name="lean4lean" />

:<math>\frac{}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Sort}\,u : \mathrm{Sort}\,(u+1)} \qquad \frac{c.\{\bar u\} : A \text{ is in Lean's environment}}{\Gamma \vdash c.\{\bar \ell\} : A[\bar\ell/\bar u]}</math>

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \mathrm{Sort}\,v}{\Gamma \vdash (x : A) \to B : \mathrm{Sort}\,(\mathrm{imax}\,u\,v)}</math>

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash e : B}{\Gamma \vdash \lambda x : A.\, e : (x : A) \to B} \qquad \frac{\Gamma \vdash f : (x : A) \to B \qquad \Gamma \vdash a : A}{\Gamma \vdash f\,a : B[a/x]}</math>

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash v : A \qquad \Gamma \vdash e[v/x] : B}{\Gamma \vdash (\mathrm{let}\ x : A := v;\ e) : B} \qquad \frac{\Gamma \vdash e : A \qquad \Gamma \vdash A \equiv B}{\Gamma \vdash e : B}</math>

The first says each universe lives in the next. The second lets a constant be used at any
instance <math>\bar\ell</math> of its universe parameters <math>\bar u</math>. The next three
are the formation, introduction and elimination rules of the dependent function type, taken
up in [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Dependent function types|Dependent function types]].
The let rule types the body with the value substituted for the variable, so the body may
rely on what the variable stands for. The last, the '''conversion rule''', says that a term
of type <math>A</math> also has every type definitionally equal to <math>A</math>. Conversion
is where computation enters typing, and it is the subject of
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Definitional equality|Definitional equality]].

Literals and projections add rules of the same kind: a natural-number literal has
type <code>Nat</code>, a string literal has type <code>String</code>, and a projection has
the type of the field it selects. Inductive types add their type formers, constructors and
recursors as constants, each with its own type
([[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Inductive types and recursors|Inductive types and recursors]]).

== Checking against inference ==

There are two ways to use the rules. '''Type inference''' takes a context and a term and
computes a type for it. '''Type checking''' takes a context, a term and a proposed type, and
decides whether the term has that type.

Lean's kernel is built around inference. For an application <code>f a</code> it infers the
type of <code>f</code>, reduces that type until a function type <math>(x : A) \to B</math>
appears, infers the type of <code>a</code>, asks whether that type is definitionally equal to
<math>A</math>, and returns <math>B[a/x]</math>. Checking a definition or theorem with stated
type <math>T</math> and value <math>v</math> is done the same way: the Lean kernel infers the type
of <math>v</math> and asks whether it is definitionally equal to <math>T</math>. For a theorem
this comparison is the heart of proof checking: the inferred type is what the proof actually proves, and
the comparison confirms that it is what was claimed.<ref name="bailey" /> The Lean kernel's
inference function also has a mode that skips the checks and only computes a type, for terms
already known to be well typed.<ref name="lean4lean" />

The elaborator uses both directions. <code>#check</code> asks it to infer:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check fun (n : Nat) => n + 1
#check (fun n => n + 1 : Int → Int)
#check let x := 2; x * x
#check (Prod.mk 1 true).2
</pre>

Lean prints <code>fun n => n + 1 : Nat → Nat</code>, then <code>fun n => n + 1 : Int → Int</code>,
then <code>let x := 2; x * x : Nat</code> (over two lines) and <code>(1, true).snd : Bool</code>.
The second term is the same text as the first, but the ascription <code>(… : Int → Int)</code>
gives the elaborator an '''expected type''' to check against, and it uses that type to decide
what <code>n</code> and <code>+</code> mean.<ref name="tpil">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura,
Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'', lean-lang.org (version for
Lean 4.33.0), chapter 2, "Dependent Type Theory".
https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Dependent-Type-Theory/</ref> When an expected
type and an inferred type disagree, elaboration fails:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : Bool := (3 : Nat)
</pre>

Lean reports:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Type mismatch
  3
has type
  Nat
but is expected to have type
  Bool
</pre>

The message names both sides of the comparison: the type inferred for the term and the type
it was checked against.

== What the judgment leaves out ==

The core language has no implicit arguments, no type classes, no pattern matching, no
recursive definitions and no tactics. All of these are features of the elaborator, which
translates them into the terms above before the Lean kernel sees anything; a recursive function,
for instance, usually reaches the Lean kernel as an application of a recursor or of a well-founded
fixed-point combinator.<ref name="refman-elab">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean
4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, sections 2.3, "The Kernel", and 2.4, "Elaboration Results".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/</ref> The division
of labour is described on [[Lean theorem prover/System/Elaboration|Elaboration]] and
[[Lean theorem prover/System/The Lean kernel|The Lean kernel]].

The rules also leave open how <math>\Gamma \vdash A \equiv B</math> is decided. In Lean's full
theory that relation is undecidable, so the Lean kernel decides a slightly smaller relation;
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Definitional equality|Definitional equality]] gives the
details and the sources.<ref name="carneiro2019" />
